findings.summary: Every page's blocks are offset roughly a third of a page ahead of its title, so each page ends by opening the next chapter's topic and the syllabus's ten chapters collapse into nine slides with "Per-Request Caching: Identity & Lifetime" never appearing as a page title at all.
findings.evidence: Page 1 ("Why GraphQL Explodes: The N+1 Problem") ends with heading "Every Field Has A Resolver" and the resolver-signature code; page 2 ("How Resolvers Actually Execute") ends with "What It Is" defining DataLoader plus the API-surface table; page 3 ("DataLoader: The Batching Primitive") opens with "Shape Of A Batch". The whole caching chapter ("Cache Before Queue", "The Diamond", "Keys Are Identity", "Controls", "Lifetime") sits on the page titled "Inside the Batch: Ticks, Queues & Scheduling", and no slide carries the title "Per-Request Caching: Identity & Lifetime".
findings.fix: Re-split the block stream on chapter boundaries: move the trailing next-chapter blocks off each page so every page starts with its own topic's opening heading, and restore the tenth page titled "Per-Request Caching: Identity & Lifetime" carrying the cache blocks currently stranded on page 4.

findings.summary: The "Constructor" card at bottom-right runs off the right edge of the page, truncating both of its code lines mid-token.
findings.evidence: Card reads "new DataLoader(batchFn, optio" and "batchFn: (keys) => Promise<(V" — both stop at the page boundary (x = 1080px) with the closing tokens missing.
findings.fix: Move the Constructor card fully inside the right margin and wrap or shrink its code lines so "new DataLoader(batchFn, options)" and "batchFn: (keys) => Promise<(V | Error)[]>" render complete.

findings.summary: The caption advertises ten pages but the carousel contains only nine.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages, from the first symptom in your logs to the production checklist." — the `titles` array (and the post's `slides` array in data/handbooks/graphql/n-plus-one/parts/01/post.json) holds 9 entries, ending at "Summary: The Complete Defense".
findings.fix: Change "Ten pages" to "Nine pages" in the caption text.

findings.summary: The "Depth Multiplies" section states an absolute rule and a query-count formula that its own example contradicts — a chain of to-one fields adds queries, it does not multiply.
findings.evidence: "`posts`, `author`, `company`, `employees` = 1+50+50+50N" and "Depth multiplies the count, it never just adds". For `posts(first:50){author{company{employees}}}` each level after `posts` is a to-one field, so the counts are 1 + 50 + 50 + 50 = 151 — strictly additive, with no `N` term at the last level.
findings.fix: Correct the formula to "= 1+50+50+50 = 151" and replace the rule with the accurate one: "To-one levels add N each; nested list levels multiply (that is where N^D comes from)", matching page 4's "Naive nesting issues N^D queries".

findings.summary: The tree-walk diagram draws `author` as a sibling of `posts` under the query root, contradicting the chapter's core claim that author resolvers run once per post parent.
findings.evidence: Diagram edges are `{"from":"n0","to":"b0"}` and `{"from":"n0","to":"b1"}` with `b0` = "posts (1 call)" and `b1` = "author (50 calls)", while the layout note asks for "query root → 50 posts → 50 author resolver calls" and the page teaches "`parent` is the resolved value one level up".
findings.fix: Re-parent the diagram so `author (50 calls)` hangs off `posts`, and hang the `user 3 / user 7 / user 3 again` nodes off the author node, making the nesting that multiplies calls visible.

findings.summary: The page claims every failed load is cached, but DataLoader explicitly does not cache batch-level failures — it clears those keys automatically.
findings.evidence: "Rejections cache too — a bad load stays bad" and "Clear in the batch catch to avoid poisoning" (page 4); repeated on page 8 as "A cached rejection poisons that key all request". The DataLoader README states: "If a batch load fails (that is, a batch function throws or returns a rejected Promise), then the requested values will not be cached" — only "if a batch function returns an `Error` instance for an individual value, that `Error` will be cached to avoid frequently loading the same `Error`."
findings.fix: Restrict the claim to per-key Errors: change the page-4 bullets to "Per-key `Error` slots are cached — that key stays bad" and "A batch that throws/rejects is auto-cleared; `clear(k)` only for cached `Error` slots", and change the page-8 bullet to "A cached `Error` slot poisons that key for the request".

findings.summary: The cacheKeyFn code line in "4. Keys Are Identity" overflows its card and is overlapped by the "Lifetime" card, hiding the end of the expression.
findings.evidence: "cacheKeyFn: k => JSON.stringify([k.tenant, k.id])" runs past the card's right border at ~x=700 and the tail "([k.tenant, k.id])" is greyed out under the Lifetime card's left edge.
findings.fix: Wrap the cacheKeyFn line onto multiple lines inside the card (or reduce its font size) so it stays within the card's width and clear of the Lifetime card.

findings.summary: The title "Inside the Batch: Ticks, Queues & Scheduling" misdescribes page 4, which is almost entirely about DataLoader's per-request cache, while the tick/queue/scheduling material actually sits on page 3.
findings.evidence: Page 4 headings after its opening bullets are "Cache Before Queue", "The Diamond", "Keys Are Identity", "Controls", "Lifetime", "The Factory Is The Pattern" (e.g. "memoization keyed by the `load()` key, checked before anything is queued"), whereas the scheduling content — "How A Batch Forms", "Default scheduler is `process.nextTick` in Node", "Loads in a later tick form a new batch", `batchScheduleFn` — appears on page 3 under "DataLoader: The Batching Primitive".
findings.fix: Retitle page 4 to name its real subject, e.g. "The Per-Request Cache: Dedup, Keys & Lifetime", and fold the ticks/queues/scheduling framing into page 3's title (e.g. "DataLoader: Batching, Ticks & Queues").

findings.summary: The priming code line in "2. Authorization And Priming" overflows the card's right edge and its tail is clipped against the background.
findings.evidence: "users.forEach(u => prime(u.id, u))" extends past the card border; "prime(u.id, u))" is rendered faded outside the card body at ~x=700.
findings.fix: Break the line after "u =>" or shorten it so the full "users.forEach(u => prime(u.id, u))" fits inside the card.

findings.summary: The "Fix" column of the "3. Breaks And Fixes" table is clipped at the table's right edge, cutting off the fix text on several rows.
findings.evidence: Fix cells show "remap via Map" (trailing token cut at the border), "Promise.all" (cut), and "hoist to context" (cut) at the table boundary ~x=712, while the adjacent "5. Driver Limits" card sits immediately to the right.

findings.evidence: Page 9's first block is bullets beginning "L4 lookahead JOINs on measured hot paths only"; the diagram `{"nodes":["schema design","static limits","DataLoader","lookahead","shared cache","backstops"]}` and "L1 schema...", "L2 static...", "L3 DataLoader..." are the last blocks of page 8.

findings.summary: The caption promises ten pages but the part contains nine slides.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages, from the first symptom in your logs to the production checklist." — the slides array holds nine entries, from "Why GraphQL Explodes" to "Summary: The Complete Defense".
findings.fix: Either restore the missing per-request-caching page (see the offset finding) or change the caption to match the delivered page count.

findings.summary: The same per-request context-factory snippet is shown twice on one page, so the closing "The Factory Is The Pattern" block teaches nothing the reader has not already seen a few blocks earlier.
findings.evidence: Page 4 block: `context: ({ req }) => ({` / `  loaders: createLoaders(db, tenant(req))` / `})` under "// fresh loaders per request", and again at the page end: `context: ({ req }) => ({` / `  loaders: createLoaders(db, tenant(req))` / `}) // fresh object of loaders per call` plus the resolver line.
findings.fix: Keep one context-factory snippet; reduce the second block to the new material only — the one-line resolver `author: (post, _, { loaders }) => loaders.userById.load(post.authorId)`.

findings.summary: The context-factory code passes `tenant(req)` into the loader factory before tenant scoping has been introduced or justified.
findings.evidence: Page 4: `loaders: createLoaders(db, tenant(req))`; the rationale appears only on page 5 — "Pass tenant scope into the loader factory" / "Never let one `IN` query span tenants".
findings.fix: Either drop the `tenant(req)` argument from the page 4 snippet (use `createLoaders(db)`) and add it back on page 5 where scoping is taught, or add a one-line note on page 4 flagging that the tenant argument is explained with the wiring chapter.

findings.summary: The "Diamond" diagram shows arrows fanning out of user 7 into two loads plus a detached "result" branch, which depicts divergence rather than the two call sites converging on a single fetch.
findings.evidence: Edges `n0→b0`, `n0→b1`, `n0→b2` with `n0` = "user 7", `b0` = "post.author", `b1` = "comment.author", `b2` = "result", and `b2→c2_0` = "one fetch", against the prose "post.author and comment.author both resolving user 7 fetch it once".
findings.fix: Redraw so `post.author` and `comment.author` are the top row, both edges point into a single `.load(7)` node, and that node points to one `SELECT ... IN` fetch.

findings.summary: Prisma is listed among tools that compile the GraphQL AST to SQL, which it does not do.
findings.evidence: "Join Monster, Prisma, Hasura, PostGraphile compile AST to SQL". Hasura, PostGraphile and Join Monster compile a GraphQL document/AST into SQL; Prisma is an ORM whose own client queries are compiled to SQL by its query engine — it never sees the GraphQL AST. The next bullet, "Prisma batches `findUnique` calls automatically", describes DataLoader-style batching, not AST compilation.
findings.fix: Drop Prisma from that list — "Join Monster, Hasura, PostGraphile compile AST to SQL" — and leave Prisma in the following bullet where its auto-batching of `findUnique` is described.

findings.summary: The driver-limit example says 5000 keys blows the parameter cap, contradicting the Postgres limit quoted in the very next bullet.
findings.evidence: "Unset `maxBatchSize` plus 5000 keys blows the cap" immediately followed by "Postgres about 65535, SQL Server 2100 params" — 5000 is well under Postgres's ~65535 bind parameters.
findings.fix: Either raise the number past the Postgres ceiling ("plus 70k keys") or scope the example to the driver it actually breaks ("plus 5000 keys blows SQL Server's 2100-param cap").
